subject: Climate & Environment
title: Sea Level Rise
description: A quick, practical guide to Sea Level Rise.

hook.text: Since 1900, global sea levels have risen about 20 centimeters. The rate is speeding up.

buildup.text: Half comes from melting ice. The other half comes from thermal expansion — warm water swells.

discovery.text: By 2100, seas could rise 0.3 to 1 meter depending on emissions choices made now.

twist.text: Even one meter would flood the homes of 200 million coastal residents worldwide.

climax.text: Island nations like Tuvalu and the Maldives could vanish entirely from the map.

punchline.text: The ocean is slowly reclaiming land we thought was ours.

quiz.question: How much have sea levels risen since 1900?

details.summary: Global sea levels have risen roughly 20 centimeters since 1900 and the rate is accelerating. Current levels rise about 3.7 millimeters per year from a combination of thermal expansion and melting glaciers and ice sheets, threatening coastal cities and small island nations.
details.whyItMatters: Sea-level rise is irreversible on human timescales and threatens hundreds of millions of people. Even modest rises amplify storm surge and erosion dramatically.
takeaways: Sea levels have risen about 20 cm since 1900
The rate has more than doubled since the 1990s
Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are now the dominant contributors

faq.question: How much could sea levels rise by 2100?
faq.answer: IPCC projections range from about 30 cm under aggressive emission cuts to over 1 meter under high-emission scenarios. If ice-sheet collapse accelerates, some studies suggest 2 meters or more is possible, though uncertain.

faq.question: Which cities are most at risk from sea-level rise?
faq.answer: Low-lying coastal megacities like Shanghai, Miami, Mumbai, Jakarta, and Dhaka face severe flooding risks. Small island nations like Tuvalu, Kiribati, and the Maldives risk becoming uninhabitable within decades.
